source_text: Ad cuius nominis cavendam invidiam, frustra omnino diversarum facis haereseon mentionem. Ais enim: Sicut Ariani Catholicos Sabellianos vocant, quamvis certam personarum distinctionem faciant, naturae tamen communione servata; ita et a nobis Manichaeorum vobis nomen imponi; cum vos non dicatis malum esse nuptias, quod dicunt Manichaei, sed dicatis malum in omnes homines naturae conditione transire [n59] . Haec autem argumenta tua prudentibus non ambigo irrisum iri; nam ut Ariani falsos Catholicos Sabellianos dicunt, cum a nobis et Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti personarum fiat sine ulla confusione et sine mutatione substantiae distinctio, illique hebetissime calumnientur, inter unum et tres nihil interesse; ita etiam Catholici iure meritoque vos Manichaeos esse pronuntiant; quia id a nobis dici fides vestra compellit. Asserunt quippe Manichaei naturalem peccatum: vos dicitis naturale. Dicunt Manichaei libidinem corporum a diabolo esse plantatam; tu id multiplicata disputatione confirmas. Contendunt illi per liberum arbitrium non posse malum caveri, quippe quod naturale sit; tu quoque iisdem sermonibus liberum commentaris arbitrium, sed per quod malum fieri possit, a malo autem non possit desisti. Dicit Manichaeus semen esse maledictum: tu id Scripturarum auctoritate probare conaris. Dicit Manichaeus inconvertibilem esse malitiam; tu sic esse vociferaris. Sed dicis tu Adam solum naturae fuisse melioris; dicit etiam Manichaeus ad Patricium, meliorem illum secutis credi oportere, quasi de primae concretum flore substantiae. Dicis tu commixtionem propter naturales motus esse diabolicam, atque homines a diabolo quasi fruticis a se plantati fructus iure decerpi; dicit etiam hoc Manichaeus, quippe a quo id credere et affirmare didicisti. Dicit Manichaeus et naturam et nuptias malas esse: tu autem bonas nuptias, sed ream naturam. Non tu hic religiosior, sed ille prudentior. Quomodo ergo falsum est, quod dicunt Ariani, Catholicos Sabellianos esse; ita verissimum est, quod dicunt Catholici, Traducianos non esse aliud quam Manichaeos; distinctionem autem inter vos illusoriam quidem, non fide vestra, sed imperitia contigisse. Unius ergo fidei tu et Manichaeus; sed ille minus impudens, quam tua gravitas invenitur; neque enim facile Manichaeus aut Melitidis alter offenditur, qui dicat se damnare naturam hominum, sed non infamare coniugia.
pass_a_gloss: For avoiding the spite of which name, you altogether in vain make mention of diverse heresies. For you say: As the Arians call the Catholics Sabellians, although they make a certain distinction of persons, the communion of nature nevertheless having been kept; so also the name of Manichaeans is imposed on you by us; when you do not say marriages are evil, which the Manichaeans say, but you say that evil passes into all humans by the condition of nature. But I do not doubt that these arguments of yours will be laughed at by the prudent; for as the Arians say false Catholics are Sabellians, when by us a distinction of the persons of both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is made without any confusion and without a change of substance, and they most dully calumniate that there is no difference between one and three; so also the Catholics by right and desert pronounce you to be Manichaeans; because your faith compels that to be said by us. For the Manichaeans assert a natural sin: you say natural. The Manichaeans say the lust of bodies was planted by the devil; you confirm that by a multiplied disputation. They contend that through free decision evil cannot be bewaired, seeing that it is natural; you also by the same speeches invent a free decision, but through which evil can be done, but from evil it cannot be desisted. Manichaeus says the seed is cursed: you try to prove that by the authority of the Scriptures. Manichaeus says malice is inconvertible; you cry out that it is so. But you say Adam alone was of a better nature; Manichaeus also says to Patricius that that one ought to be believed better than those following, as if concreted from the flower of the first substance. You say mingling on account of natural motions is diabolical, and that humans are plucked by right by the devil as fruits of a shrub planted by himself; Manichaeus also says this, seeing that from him you learned to believe and affirm it. Manichaeus says both nature and marriages are evil: you however good marriages, but a guilty nature. You are not here more religious, but he more prudent. How therefore it is false that the Arians say Catholics are Sabellians; so it is most true that the Catholics say Traducians are nothing other than Manichaeans; but the distinction between you, illusory indeed, happened not by your faith but by unskillfulness. Of one faith therefore you and Manichaeus; but he is found less shameless than your gravity; for not easily is a Manichaeus or another of Melitis offended, who would say he condemns the nature of humans, but does not infame marriages.

pass_b_english: To avoid the odium of this name, your mention of various heresies is entirely futile. You say: ‘Just as Arians call catholics Sabellians, although catholics distinguish the persons clearly while preserving their common nature, so you impose the Manichaeans’ name on us, although we do not say marriage is evil, as Manichaeans do, but say evil passes into all human beings as a condition of nature’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.23.38). I have no doubt the wise will laugh at these arguments. Arians falsely call catholics Sabellians, since we distinguish the persons of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit without any confusion or change of substance, while they very stupidly slander us as though one and three were no different. Likewise, catholics most rightly declare you Manichaeans, because your creed compels us to say so.

Manichaeans assert natural sin; you say it is natural. They say the devil planted bodily desire; you confirm this through extended argument. They contend that evil cannot be avoided through free will because it is natural. With the same words you too invent a free will through which evil can be done, but evil cannot be abandoned. Mani says seed is cursed; you try to prove it by scriptural authority. Mani says wickedness cannot be changed; you shout that it is so. But you say Adam alone possessed a better nature. Mani too, writing to Patricius, says Adam should be believed better than those who followed, as though formed from the flower of the first substance. You say intercourse is diabolical because of its natural movements, and human beings are rightly plucked by the devil like fruit from a shrub he planted. Mani says this too: he is, indeed, the one from whom you learned to believe and affirm it. Mani says both nature and marriage are evil. You say marriage is good but nature guilty. You are not more religious here; he is more intelligent.

Just as it is false when Arians say catholics are Sabellians, then, it is entirely true when catholics say advocates of inherited sin are nothing other than Manichaeans. The illusory distinction between you arises not from your creed but from your ignorance. You and Mani therefore hold one faith, but he proves less shameless than your distinguished self. For one does not readily meet either a Manichaean or another Melitides who says he condemns human nature without slandering marriage.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's pudenda libido is the appetite accompanying union, not a created substance of sin.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
